name: Adrammelek
title: Son of King Sennacherib who participated in the murder of his father
summary: Adrammelek was the son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib. Together with his brother Sharezer, he killed their father while he was worshiping in the temple of the god Nisroch in Nineveh. After the patricide, the two brothers fled to the land of Ararat, and it was their brother Esarhaddon who took over the Assyrian throne. The murder occurred following Sennacherib's failed campaign against Jerusalem, where an angel of the Lord struck down the Assyrian army. The biblical authors portray Sennacherib's violent end as a divine judgment on the proud great king who had mocked the God of Israel. The name Adrammelek also appears in 2 Kings 17:31 as a designation for an idol worshiped by the people from Sepharvaim, but this is a different figure than the crown prince.

keyEvents.title: Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Adrammelek's father Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem during King Hezekiah's reign, but God intervened and an angel struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers. Sennacherib had to retreat to Nineveh. This humiliation forms the background for what later happened to Sennacherib.

keyEvents.title: The murder of Sennacherib
keyEvents.description: Adrammelek and his brother Sharezer killed their father Sennacherib while he was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch in Nineveh. They then fled to the land of Ararat. The event is presented as a fulfillment of God's judgment against the proud Assyrian king.

keyEvents.title: Esarhaddon takes the throne
keyEvents.description: After Adrammelech and Sharezer had killed their father and fled, their brother Esarhaddon took the Assyrian throne. The patricide did not lead to Adrammelech gaining power himself, but instead paved the way for another heir's accession.

keyEvents.title: The idol Adrammelech in Samaria
keyEvents.description: The name Adrammelech is also associated with an idol worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim in Samaria after the Assyrians settled them there. They sacrificed their children in fire to this idol. This is a different figure from the person Adrammelech, but the similarity in names is worth noting.

keyEvents.title: Parallel account in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: The murder of Sennacherib is also mentioned in 2 Chronicles. Here, Adrammelech is not named by name, but it is reported that some of Sennacherib's own sons killed him with swords, and that Esarhaddon became king after him.

versions.reason: [minor] The title is accurate but could be more descriptive to distinguish the person Adrammelek from the idol name. A small clarification may be helpful.; [major] The role "warrior" is not well documented in the Bible for Adrammelek. He is primarily known as a fratricide and king's son. The Bible does not describe him as a warrior, but as a prince who killed his father. Roles should reflect what the Bible actually tells us about him.; [minor] The summary mixes two different "Adrammeleks": the person (Sennacherib's son) and the idol. Although this may be useful information, it should be clarified that these are two completely different entities sharing a name.; [minor] The event "Adrammelek as an idol in Samaria" concerns an idol, not the person Adrammelek. footnotes.text: The name Adrammelech (Hebrew: אַדְרַמֶּלֶךְ) is likely derived from the Akkadian 'Adad-milki' or 'Adar-malik', meaning 'Adad/Adar is king'. This links the name to Mesopotamian deity worship and the Assyrian religious context.

The murder of Sennacherib in 681 BC is well attested in Assyrian sources. Esarhaddon's own inscription (Prism B) tells of his brothers' rebellion and his own accession to the throne. Babylonian chronicles also mention the event.

There is debate among scholars regarding the identification of Adrammelech in Assyrian records. Some identify him with Arda-Mulissu (Arad-Ninlil), who is mentioned in Assyrian texts as one of Sennacherib's sons involved in the conspiracy. This identification is not definitively settled, but it is the most widely accepted hypothesis.

The idol Adrammelech mentioned in 2 Kings 17:31 was worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim and is likely a variant of the Mesopotamian god Adad-milki. Child sacrifice was part of the cult, which biblical authors strongly condemn as an abominable practice.

Sennacherib's campaign against Judah in 701 BC is documented in Sennacherib's own annals (the Taylor Prism), where he boasts of having besieged Jerusalem. The biblical and Assyrian sources provide complementary perspectives on this event, even though they naturally emphasize different aspects.

The land of Ararat, to which Adrammelech and Sharezer fled after the murder, corresponds to the region known in Assyrian records as Urartu – a kingdom in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia. It was a well-known rival of Assyria, which may explain why the sons sought refuge there.

According to rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 96a), Sennacherib was killed by his sons as a result of an oath he had sworn against God. This tradition highlights the theological theme of divine retribution against those who threaten His people.
